summary.text: After clearing the factorial, the proof excludes composite \(n\) by \(p\)-adic valuations: for \(n=2^k\), the exact value \(v_2((2^k-1)!)=2^k-k-1\) forces \(v_2(a(2^k-1))=k-1\), contradicting the required divisibility by \(2^k\); for an odd prime factor \(p\mid n\), counting exponents divisible by \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\), with an extra factor of \(p\) at exponent \(p\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\), gives a lower bound for \(\sum v_p(2^j-1)\) incompatible with the factorial valuation. Once \(n\) is prime, if \(d=\operatorname{ord}_n(2)<n-1\), then \(n\mid 2^d-1\) makes \(n\) divide the product in the cleared identity, while the hypothesis then forces \(n\mid(n-1)!\), a contradiction; hence \(d=n-1\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 a(r)=\frac{2^{r-1}}{r!}\prod_{j=1}^{r-1}(2^j-1)\qquad(r\geq 1).
\]
We shall use this expression as an integer. The required integrality, in the precise range needed below, will be proved first.

For a prime \(p\) and a positive integer \(x\), write \(v_p(x)\) for the exponent of \(p\) in \(x\). We use the following standard facts.

1. Legendre's formula gives
\[
 v_p(D!)=\sum_{i\geq 1}\left\lfloor\frac D{p^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
Consequently, for \(D>0\),
\[
 (p-1)v_p(D!)<D. \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, the sum in Legendre's formula is strictly less than the infinite geometric sum
\[
 \sum_{i\geq1}\frac D{p^i}=\frac D{p-1}.
\]

2. If \(p\) is odd and
\[
 o=\operatorname{ord}_p(2)
\]
is the multiplicative order of \(2\) modulo \(p\), then \(o\mid p-1\), and in particular
\[
 2\leq o\leq p-1. \tag{2}
\]
Moreover,
\[
 p\mid 2^j-1 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad o\mid j. \tag{3}
\]

3. Divisibility of nonzero positive integers can be tested prime by prime: \(X\mid Y\) if and only if \(v_p(X)\leq v_p(Y)\) for every prime \(p\).

We first establish the exact integral form of the sequence that will be used throughout. Let \(n>2\), and put \(D=n-1\). We claim that
\[
 D!\mid 2^{D-1}\prod_{j=1}^{D-1}(2^j-1). \tag{4}
\]
For \(p=2\), (1) says
\[
 v_2(D!)<D,
\]
so, since this valuation is an integer,
\[
 v_2(D!)\leq D-1=v_2(2^{D-1}).
\]
Every factor \(2^j-1\) is odd, so this is enough for the prime \(2\).

Now let \(p\) be odd and let \(o=\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\). From (1) and \(o\leq p-1\),
\[
 o\,v_p(D!)\leq (p-1)v_p(D!)\leq D-1.
\]
Since \(o>0\), this implies
\[
 v_p(D!)\leq \left\lfloor\frac{D-1}{o}\right\rfloor. \tag{5}
\]
Among the indices \(1,2,\ldots,D-1\), exactly \(\lfloor(D-1)/o\rfloor\) are multiples of \(o\). By (3), each corresponding factor \(2^j-1\) is divisible by \(p\). Therefore
\[
 v_p\!\left(\prod_{j=1}^{D-1}(2^j-1)\right)
 =\sum_{j=1}^{D-1}v_p(2^j-1)
 \geq \left\lfloor\frac{D-1}{o}\right\rfloor. \tag{6}
\]
Equations (5) and (6) prove the required valuation inequality for every odd prime. Thus (4) follows.

It follows in particular that the defining quotient for \(a(n-1)\) is exact, and we have the integer identity
\[
 a(n-1)(n-1)!
 =2^{n-2}\prod_{j=1}^{n-2}(2^j-1). \tag{7}
\]
For brevity, set
\[
 P_n=\prod_{j=1}^{n-2}(2^j-1),\qquad F_n=(n-1)!.
\]
Then (7) is
\[
 a(n-1)F_n=2^{n-2}P_n. \tag{8}
\]
All quantities in (8) are positive.

We now assume throughout that
\[
 n>2\quad\text{and}\quad n\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}. \tag{9}
\]
We first prove that \(n\) is prime.

Suppose, for a contradiction, that \(n\) is composite. There are two exhaustive possibilities: either every prime divisor of \(n\) is \(2\), in which case \(n\) is a power of \(2\), or \(n\) has an odd prime divisor.

### Case 1: \(n\) is a power of \(2\)

Write
\[
 n=2^k.
\]
Since \(n>2\), we have \(k\geq2\). Taking \(2\)-adic valuations in (8), and observing that every factor of \(P_n\) is odd, gives
\[
 v_2(a(2^k-1))+v_2((2^k-1)!)=2^k-2. \tag{10}
\]
We calculate the factorial valuation exactly. By Legendre's formula,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 v_2((2^k-1)!)
 &=\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}\left\lfloor\frac{2^k-1}{2^i}\right\rfloor\\
 &=\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}(2^{k-i}-1)\\
 &=(2^k-2)-(k-1)\\
 &=2^k-k-1.
\end{aligned} \tag{11}
\]
(The terms for \(i\geq k\) are zero.) Substituting (11) into (10) yields
\[
 v_2(a(2^k-1))=k-1. \tag{12}
\]

On the other hand, for \(k\geq2\),
\[
 k\leq 2^k-2. \tag{13}
\]
This follows immediately by induction, beginning with equality at \(k=2\). Hence
\[
 2^k\mid 2^{2^k-2}.
\]
The hypothesis (9), with \(n=2^k\), says
\[
 2^k\mid a(2^k-1)+2^{2^k-2}.
\]
Subtracting the second summand, which is already divisible by \(2^k\), gives
\[
 2^k\mid a(2^k-1).
\]
Thus \(v_2(a(2^k-1))\geq k\), contradicting (12). Therefore a composite \(n\) satisfying (9) cannot be a power of \(2\).

### Case 2: \(n\) has an odd prime divisor

Let \(p\) be an odd prime dividing \(n\), and write
\[
 n=pm.
\]
Because \(n\) is assumed composite, \(m\neq1\), so \(m\geq2\).

Since \(p\mid n\), hypothesis (9) implies
\[
 p\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}. \tag{14}
\]
We claim that
\[
 p\nmid a(n-1). \tag{15}
\]
Indeed, if \(p\mid a(n-1)\), then (14) would imply \(p\mid2^{n-2}\). Since \(p\) is prime, this would force \(p\mid2\), contrary to \(p\neq2\).

Take \(p\)-adic valuations in (8). Because \(p\nmid a(n-1)\) and \(p\nmid2^{n-2}\), the valuations of these two factors are zero. Therefore
\[
 v_p((n-1)!)
 =v_p(P_n)
 =\sum_{j=1}^{n-2}v_p(2^j-1). \tag{16}
\]
We shall show that the right side of (16) is strictly larger than the left side.

Let again
\[
 o=\operatorname{ord}_p(2).
\]
For any positive integer \(D\), the argument used in (5) and (6) gives
\[
 v_p(D!)\leq\left\lfloor\frac{D-1}{o}\right\rfloor \tag{17}
\]
and
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^{D-1}v_p(2^j-1)
 \geq\left\lfloor\frac{D-1}{o}\right\rfloor. \tag{18}
\]
We need one strengthened version of (18). If
\[
 op\leq D-1, \tag{19}
\]
then
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^{D-1}v_p(2^j-1)
 \geq\left\lfloor\frac{D-1}{o}\right\rfloor+1. \tag{20}
\]
To see this, (18) counts one factor of \(p\) for every multiple of \(o\). At the particular multiple \(op\), there are in fact at least two factors of \(p\). Namely, put \(x=2^o\). Since \(x\equiv1\pmod p\), both factors on the right of
\[
 x^p-1=(x-1)(1+x+x^2+\cdots+x^{p-1})
\]
are divisible by \(p\): the first because \(x\equiv1\pmod p\), and the second because it is congruent to \(p\equiv0\pmod p\). Thus
\[
 p^2\mid 2^{op}-1,
\]
which supplies one valuation beyond the baseline count and proves (20).

Apply these estimates with
\[
 D=n-1=pm-1,
\]
so that \(D-1=pm-2\). We split according as \(p\leq m\) or \(p>m\).

#### Subcase 2a: \(p\leq m\)

Using \(o\leq p-1\),
\[
 op\leq(p-1)p=p^2-p.
\]
Since \(p\leq m\), we have \(p^2\leq pm\), and because the odd prime \(p\geq3\),
\[
 p^2-p\leq pm-2.
\]
Thus \(op\leq pm-2=D-1\), so the strengthened estimate (20) applies:
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^{pm-2}v_p(2^j-1)
 \geq \left\lfloor\frac{pm-2}{o}\right\rfloor+1. \tag{21}
\]
But (17) gives
\[
 v_p((pm-1)!)\leq \left\lfloor\frac{pm-2}{o}\right\rfloor. \tag{22}
\]
Equations (21) and (22) contradict the equality (16).

#### Subcase 2b: \(p>m\)

Here \(m<p\), so
\[
 pm-1<p^2.
\]
Legendre's formula therefore has only its first possibly nonzero term and gives, in fact,
\[
 v_p((pm-1)!)=\left\lfloor\frac{pm-1}{p}\right\rfloor=m-1. \tag{23}
\]
For the product side, \(o\leq p-1\) and \(m\geq2\) imply
\[
 om\leq(p-1)m=pm-m\leq pm-2.
\]
Consequently
\[
 m\leq\left\lfloor\frac{pm-2}{o}\right\rfloor.
\]
Using (18),
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^{pm-2}v_p(2^j-1)
 \geq\left\lfloor\frac{pm-2}{o}\right\rfloor
 \geq m. \tag{24}
\]
This contradicts (16) and (23), since the factorial side is only \(m-1\).

Both subcases are impossible. Thus a composite \(n\) can satisfy neither Case 1 nor Case 2. We conclude that
\[
 n\text{ is prime}. \tag{25}
\]

It remains to prove that \(2\) is a primitive root modulo \(n\). Since \(n>2\) is prime, \(2\) is nonzero modulo \(n\), and Fermat's theorem shows that its multiplicative order
\[
 d=\operatorname{ord}_n(2)
\]
is a positive divisor of \(n-1\). Thus \(d\leq n-1\). Suppose, for a contradiction, that \(d<n-1\). Then
\[
 1\leq d\leq n-2. \tag{26}
\]
By the definition of multiplicative order,
\[
 2^d\equiv1\pmod n,
\]
so
\[
 n\mid2^d-1. \tag{27}
\]
Because the index \(d\) occurs among \(1,2,\ldots,n-2\), the number \(2^d-1\) is one of the factors of \(P_n\). Hence (27) gives
\[
 n\mid P_n. \tag{28}
\]

Now multiply the assumed divisibility (9) by \(F_n=(n-1)!\). We obtain
\[
 n\mid (a(n-1)+2^{n-2})F_n. \tag{29}
\]
Using (8), the expression on the right can be rewritten as
\[
\begin{aligned}
 (a(n-1)+2^{n-2})F_n
 &=a(n-1)F_n+2^{n-2}F_n\\
 &=2^{n-2}P_n+2^{n-2}F_n\\
 &=2^{n-2}(P_n+F_n). 
\end{aligned} \tag{30}
\]
Since \(n\) is an odd prime, it does not divide \(2^{n-2}\). Euclid's lemma applied to (29) and (30) therefore yields
\[
 n\mid P_n+F_n. \tag{31}
\]
Together with \(n\mid P_n\) from (28), subtraction gives
\[
 n\mid F_n=(n-1)!. \tag{32}
\]
This is impossible: none of the factors \(1,2,\ldots,n-1\) is divisible by the prime \(n\), so their product is not divisible by \(n\).

The contradiction shows that \(d\) cannot be smaller than \(n-1\). Since already \(d\leq n-1\), we have
\[
 \operatorname{ord}_n(2)=n-1.
\]
For prime \(n\), Euler's totient is \(\varphi(n)=n-1\). Thus \(2\) has order \(\varphi(n)\) modulo \(n\), which is exactly the assertion that \(2\) is a primitive root modulo \(n\).

Therefore, for every integer \(n>2\),
\[
 n\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}
\]
implies that \(n\) is prime and that \(2\) is a primitive root modulo \(n\), as required.
